title: CSS Units and Values
summary: CSS units tell the browser how to measure a size or space. Some use a fixed amount, and others depend on nearby sizes.
introduction: CSS units tell the browser how to measure a size or space. Some use a fixed amount, and others depend on nearby sizes. Compare pixels, percentages and rem units. Change the screen or text size and see which measurements change with it.
learningObjectives: Choose between px, em, rem, % and viewport units for a given property
Explain how em compounds and why rem is predictable
Compute values with calc() and keep them within limits using clamp()

blocks.text: The only absolute unit you will use on screen is the pixel, `px`. A CSS pixel is a reference unit (1/96 of an inch), not a physical dot, which is why `16px` text looks about the same size on a cheap monitor and a high-density phone. Pixels are right for things that should not scale: hairline borders, box shadows, tiny offsets. `cm`, `mm`, `in` and `pt` exist for print stylesheets.

blocks.text: Because `em` is relative to the *parent's* font size when used on `font-size`, nested elements multiply. A list item set to `1.2em` inside another `1.2em` list item is 1.44 times the base size, and a third level is 1.728 times. `rem` always refers to the root, so `1.2rem` is the same size at every depth.

blocks.text: Compounding is a feature when you want it: `padding: 1em` on a button means the padding grows with the button's text, so a large button is spacious and a small one compact, with one rule. For font sizes, use `rem`.

blocks.title: Do not fix the root font size in pixels
blocks.text: `html { font-size: 10px; }` makes the rem arithmetic easy (1rem = 10px) but it overrides the font size the user chose in their browser settings, which people with low vision depend on. Leave the root at `100%` and use the real values (`1.25rem` is 20px), or if you must have the 10px base use `font-size: 62.5%`, which still scales with the user's setting.

A percentage refers to the same property of the containing block: `width: 50%` is half the parent's width. `height: 100%` only works when the parent has an explicit height, which is why full-screen sections use viewport units instead: `height: 100vh` is the full viewport height. On phones the browser's toolbars appear and disappear, so `100vh` can be taller than the visible area; `100dvh` (dynamic viewport height) follows the visible area. Viewport units are also what makes text *fluid*: `font-size: 4vw` grows and shrinks with the window, but with no limit, which is where the next section comes in.
Math functions: calc(), min(), max() and clamp()

`calc()` does arithmetic and may mix units: `calc(100% - 2rem)` is the parent's width minus a fixed margin. `min()` takes the smallest of its arguments, `max()` the largest, and `clamp(minimum, preferred, maximum)` keeps a preferred value within two limits. Together they replace many media queries. One syntax rule to remember: the `+` and `-` operators must have spaces around them.
Run it and resize the browser window: the heading scales smoothly between its limits, and the page keeps a margin on narrow screens without a single media query.

Some values are plain numbers. `line-height: 1.5` is a multiplier of the element's own font size and is the recommended way to write it. `0` needs no unit (`margin: 0`). `opacity`, `flex`, `z-index` and `font-weight` are unitless. Angles use `deg` or `turn` (`rotate(90deg)`), durations use `s` or `ms` (`transition: 200ms`), and resolutions in media queries use `dppx`.

questions.question: With the root font size at its default, how large is `font-size: 1.5rem`?
questions.explanation: The default root font size is 16px, and rem is always relative to the root, so 1.5rem is 24px regardless of nesting.
options: It depends on the parent's font size

questions.question: `font-size: ___(1rem, 2vw, 2rem);` keeps a fluid value between a minimum and a maximum.
questions.explanation: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` returns the preferred value but never less than the minimum or more than the maximum.
